gaz_identification: Bela, Las Bela (Mirchandani's Armābel for 阿點婆翅羅)
local_evidence: In the 7th century the ruler of Armanbel, believed to be Bela, was a Buddhist Samani descended from agents of Rai Sahiras; Chach marched to Bela c. 635-6 to fix the Kirman boundary and was received loyally, then passed into Makran.
quote: the ruler of Armanbel, which is believed to be the town of Bela, was a u Buddhist … Samani descended from the agents of Rai Sahiras … Chach was cordially received at Bela
note: p. 23 (Buddhist period). Mirchandani's main support for Las Bela = 阿點婆翅羅: a Buddhist ruler subject to Sind c. 635, matching 統屬信度國 and a Buddhist country; but the gazetteer only "believes" Armabel = Bela. No Xuanzang link.

gaz_identification: Bela as Arab base on the Makran–Sind route
local_evidence: Muhammad bin Qasim entered Makran early in the 8th century and marched through Bela; the governor of Makran died there; Qasim used Bela as a base for an advance inland; Buddhism probably gave way to Islam then.
quote: Buddhism probably gave … Muhammad Qilsim returned to Bela … which he seems to have used as a base for an advance into … the interior of the country
note: pp. 23-24. Puts Bela on the main Makran–Sind road, as Mirchandani's route requires; the "Buddhism gave place to Islam" is inference, not evidence.

gaz_identification: Bela = ancient Armabel, or Khairo Kot (Khaira Bela) in Sheh-Liari
local_evidence: Bela was known to the ancients as Armael/Armabel; native histories call it Kara Bela, so the ancient town may be another mound, notably Khairo Kot (Khaira Bela) in Sheh-Liari; Armabel was taken by Rai Chach c. 631 and later by Muhammad bin Qasim.
quote: To the ancients it was known … as Armael, Annabel, or Arm&bil … the country, notably Khairo Kot or Khaira Bdla in the … Annabel was taken by Rai Chach during … his expedition to Makran, about 631 A.D.
note: p. 207-208 (Bela, miniature gazetteer). The gazetteer itself doubts the Bela = Armabel equation and offers Khairo Kot ("old Bela", p. 7), not Mirchandani's Gondakahar, as the site of the old town.

gaz_identification: Ancient town S of Badho and W of Gagu, by local tradition Armabel
local_evidence: Sheh-Liari niabat is rich in ancient sites on the old Makran–Sind line; Kuchli Bandar may be an Arab-period port; a site south of Badho and west of Gagu near the Hor is connected by local tradition with Armabel.
quote: rich in ancient sites, probably owing to its situation on the … old line of communication between Makran and Sind … Local tradition connects this with the Armabela or
note: p. 198. A third candidate site for Armabel, near the coast (Miani Hor), south of Bela; further weakens any firm Bela/Gondakahar placement of the capital.

gaz_identification: Cave city 9 miles N of Bela, unexplored
local_evidence: About 9 miles north of Bela in the Porali gorge is an excavated cave city (Shuhr Roghun) of perhaps 1,500 dwellings hewn in conglomerate, each a verandah room and inner chamber with lamp niches, once plastered; the district gazetteer does not call them Buddhist and says they were never thoroughly explored.
quote: These interesting cave dwellings have never yet been … thoroughly explored … About 9 miles to the northward of Beyla … There are niches for lamps … I think there cannot be … less altogether than 1,500
note: pp. 37-40. The nearest notable antiquity to Mirchandani's capital Gondakahar (11 mi NW of Bela); the IGI (B-row Gondrani) calls them possibly Buddhist. Undated; no stūpa or image reported.

gaz_identification: Hinglaj shrine on the Hingol, Las Bela
local_evidence: Best-known pilgrimage in Baluchistan, below Hinglaj peak on the Hingol: a goddess called Nani by Muslims and Parbati, Kali or Mata by Hindus, in a natural cavity through whose cleft pilgrims creep; Holdich says it is celebrated from the Euphrates to the Ganges.
quote: dedicated to a goddess known as … N&ni by Muhammadans and Parbati, Kali or M&ta by … Hindus … through which pilgrims creep on all fours … celebrated from the Euphrates to the Ganges
note: pp. 35-36. A Devī (not liṅga) tīrtha on the Las Bela–Makran border; antiquity not documented here. Possible Śaiva/Śākta context for the coast west of the Indus (11.18/11.19), but no link to 大自在天祠 or Sthūleśvara.

gaz_identification: Pilgrim stations incl. Gorakhji-ki-dhuni
local_evidence: Pilgrims assemble at Karachi and are led via Miani by a Brahman agwa; 15 sacred stations en route; besides Hinglaj they visit Chaurasi, Guru Nanak-ka-saran, Gorakhji-ki-dhuni and Jholi Jhar.
quote: The other places visited by pilgrims to Hinglaj are Ohaurasi, Guru N&nak-kasar&n, Gorakhji-ki-dhuni and Jholi Jk&r
note: pp. 36-37. Nāth (Gorakh) and Hindu stations along the coastal road from Karachi; modern practice, no early date.

gaz_identification: Mud volcanoes on the coast held sacred by Hindus
local_evidence: Hindus treat the coastal mud volcanoes as the abode of a deity and consult them; one story makes them 84 pieces of a ball of ashes thrown down in anger by Siva.
quote: they spring from 84 … parts of a ball of ashes thrown to the ground in a paroxysm … of anger by Siva
note: p. 12. Minor Śaiva lore on the Las Bela coast (Hinglaj route); no date.

gaz_identification: Las Bela State: 7th-c. Buddhist ruler
local_evidence: The ruler of Las Bela in the 7th century was a Buddhist priest; the country lay on Muhammad bin Qasim's route and Buddhism probably gave way to Islam then.
quote: seventh century was a Buddhist priest. The country lay on … the route followed by the Arab general, Muhammad bin Kasim
note: pp. 188 (IGI Baluchistan). Summary of the district gazetteer's Chachnāma point; supports a Buddhist Las Bela c. 635.

gaz_identification: Caves N of Bela possibly of Buddhist origin
local_evidence: The caves at Gondrani north of Bela, hewn out of conglomerate, are possibly of Buddhist origin; with Hinglaj and Shah Bilawal the chief antiquities of the State.
quote: Gondrani, north of Bela, hewn out of the solid conglomerate … rock and possibly of Buddhist origin
note: p. 189 (also p. 22 "curious cave-city of Gondrani"). The only Buddhist attribution of the caves in these volumes, tentative; near Mirchandani's Gondakahar.

gaz_identification: Shrine of the goddess Nani/Parbati/Kali/Mata
local_evidence: Best-known pilgrimage in Baluchistan on the Hingol in Las Bela; goddess Nani (Muslim) or Parbati, Kali, Mata (Hindu); pilgrims from Karachi.
quote: The best-known place of pilgrimage in Baluchistan … known as Nani by Muhammadans and Parbatl, Kali, or Mata … by Hindus
note: pp. 192-193. Repeats the district gazetteer.

gaz_identification: Makran conquered by Rai Chach of Sind (635-6)
local_evidence: In 635-6 Rai Chach marched from Sind and conquered Makran; the Rai dynasty extended north towards Kandahar; the Arabs reached Makran as early as 643.
quote: Rai Chach marched from Sind and … conquered Makran. The Rai dynasty at the same time appear … The Arabs reached Makran as early as the year 643
note: p. 12. Makran under Sind at Xuanzang's time; Xuanzang however says 狼揭羅 was subject to Persia (役屬波剌斯), which fits a western (Persian) Makran or a post-642 situation better than Sind control.

name_in_gaz: Turan (Jhalawan), capital Khuzdar; Nudha or Budha (Kachhi)
gaz_identification: Arab-period Turan = Jhalawan, capital Khuzdar; Budha = Kachhi
local_evidence: The parts of Baluchistan best known to the Arabs were Turan (the Jhalawan country) with its capital at Khuzdar, and Nudha or Budha (Kachhi).
quote: Turan (the Jhalawan countrj’), with its … capital at Khuzdar, and Nfidha or Budha (Kachhi)
note: p. 12. The equations Mirchandani uses (Turan/Kusdar for 臂多勢羅, Budha/Kandabil for 阿軬荼) are standard here; no Xuanzang link.

gaz_identification: Kaikanan probably modern Nal (Jhalawan)
local_evidence: When Ibn Haukal visited India c. 976 he found an Arab governor residing in Kaikanan, probably the modern Nal, and governing Khuzdar.
quote: he found an Arab governor residing in Kaikanan (probably the
note: p. 12 (also p. 171: "Kaikanan, probably the modem Nal"). Places Kaikanan in Jhalawan near Khuzdar, not in Quetta-Pishin (Mirchandani) nor Waziristan (Stein); see note on 稽疆那.

gaz_identification: Kandabil probably Gandava, capital of Kachhi
local_evidence: In the 7th century Rai Chach took the capital of Kachhi, Kandabil, probably Gandava; the Arabs called the country Nadha or Budha and despoiled Kandabil several times.
quote: In the seventh century Rai Chach took its capital … Kandabil, probably Gandava. To the Arabs the country was … known as Nadha or Budha
note: p. 165. Basis of Mirchandani's 阿軬荼 = Budha, capital Kandabil = Gandava; "probably".

gaz_identification: Buddhist remains in Kachhi
local_evidence: Buddhist remains have been discovered at Chhalgari and Tambu in Kachhi; many mounds would repay excavation.
quote: Buddhist remains have been discovered at Chhalgari and … would probably repay excavation
note: p. 165-166 (also p. 22: "At Chhalgari in Kachhi are indications of interesting Buddhist remains"; p. 153). See the Kachhi gazetteer rows for detail.

gaz_identification: Gandava paid horses to Rai Chach
local_evidence: Baluchistan was noted for horses already in the 7th century, when Rai Chach of Sind took tribute in horses from Gandava.
quote: Rai Chach of Sind took tribute in … horses from Gandava
note: p. 38. Gandava subject (tributary) to Sind c. 635, like Xuanzang's 阿軬荼 (屬信度國)? Xuanzang does not say whom 阿軬荼 obeyed; weak.

gaz_identification: Jhalawan = Arab Turan, capital Khuzdar, HQ of the Arab frontier general
local_evidence: Jhalawan passed in the 7th century from the Rai dynasty of Sind to the Arabs, who called it Turan; its capital Khuzdar was the headquarters of the Arab general commanding the Indian frontier; Kaikanan, probably Nal, was another important place.
quote: dynasty of Sind to the Arabs, by whom it was known as Turan … Its capital was Khuzdar, which place was also the head
note: p. 171. Khuzdar important under the Arabs; nothing on its state before Chach. Supports Mirchandani's Turan only as a political unit of the 7th c.

gaz_identification: Coins of Marwan II (AD 745) at Dabar Kot
local_evidence: Near Dabar Kot in Loralai several coins of the Caliph Marwan II, struck at Balkh in AH 128 (AD 745), have been found.
quote: Near Dabar Kot in the Loralai District several coins … of the time of the Caliph Marwan II
note: p. 22. Shows the Duki–Thal plain on a trade route in the 8th c.; nothing pre-Islamic for Mirchandani's 伐剌拏 near Duki.

gaz_identification: Afghans = Opokien of Hiuen Tsiang (Cunningham)
local_evidence: Cunningham identifies the Afghans with the Opokien of Hiuen Tsiang in the 7th century.
quote: are also identifiable with the Opokien of Hiuen Tsiang in the
note: p. 28. Opokien = 阿薄健 of the Life (Cien zhuan), passed between 伐剌拏 (11.23) and 漕矩吒 (12.01); not in places.tsv. Only Xuanzang mentions in these seven volumes are this and the Zhob passage.

gaz_identification: Zhob as home of the Afghans in Hiuen Tsiang's time
local_evidence: Zhob, cradle of the Afghan race: Hiuen Tsiang describes the Afghans as living here in the 7th century.
quote: Hiuen Tsiang describes the Afghans … a.s living here in the seventh century
note: p. 102 (Zhob District). Places the Life's 阿薄健 in Zhob, i.e. on a Gomal/Zhob route NW of Bannu, consistent with the study's Bannu for 11.23 rather than Mirchandani's Duki.

gaz_identification: Buddhism flourished after the Sakas, many traces
local_evidence: About the time of the Sakas (2nd c. BC) Buddhism, of which many traces are still to be found, flourished in Baluchistan; the Sasanians later conquered it under Nausherwan.
quote: this time Buddhism, of which many traces are still to be found, … flourished in Baluchistan
note: p. 12. General; the "traces" cited elsewhere are Chhalgari/Tambu (Kachhi) and Gondrani (possible).

gaz_identification: Kaikanan near Kalat, perhaps Nal
local_evidence: The Rai dynasty of Sind is said to have ruled as far as Kandahar, Seistan, and the Sulaiman and Kaikanan hills; the position of Kaikanan is not determined but was near Kalat.
quote: The exact position of Kaikdndn has not been … determined, but it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of … Kaldt
note: Sarawan p. 23. Puts Kaikanan in the Kalat–Jhalawan highlands, south of Quetta; the Jhalawan section (p. 34) and the Nal entry make it Nal.

gaz_identification: Arab conquest of Khuzdar and Turan c. 664
local_evidence: c. 658 the Arabs under Taghar bin Dair from Makran reduced Kaikanan; c. 664 they captured Khuzdar and occupied Turan or Jhalawan; parts best known to them were Turan with its capital Khuzdar and Nudha or Budha (Kachhi).
quote: the Arabs captured Khuzdar and occupied the ♦surrounding … country of Tiiran or Jhalawda
note: Sarawan p. 24 (OCR "604" for 664). Arab-period frame for Mirchandani's 臂多勢羅 = Turan.

gaz_identification: Chach's march Armabel → Jhalawan → Kandabil; Kandabil = Gandava
local_evidence: Chach marched from Armabel (Bela), apparently via Jhalawan, to Kandabil and camped on the Sini (Nari?); Kandabil is identifiable with Gandava; the Arabs found Turks holding the tract between Khuzdar and Gandava; Kaikan, identified with Nal, lay in it.
quote: from Armabt^l (B^la), apparently via the Jhalawdn country … to Kandabil … There can be little doubt that Kandabil is identifiable … with the modern Ganddva
note: Kachhi p. 24. The same Bela→Jhalawan→Gandava sequence Mirchandani maps onto 阿點婆翅羅 → 臂多勢羅 → 阿軬荼; but Xuanzang's order is 臂多勢羅 (700 li N) then 阿軬荼 (300 li NE), whereas Khuzdar–Gandava is far more than 300 li (Mirchandani emends to 500).

gaz_identification: Kandabil on an elevated site, capital of Budha, ten marches from Multan
local_evidence: Biladuri puts Kandabil on a hill or elevated site, matching Gandava; it was capital of Budha (or Nudha), ten marches through the desert from Multan; the people (Jats) lived in reed huts and bred two-humped camels; Nudha is probably the correct name.
quote: Kandabil w’«is also described as the capital … of Budha (or Nudha according to some geographers)
note: Kachhi p. 24. The gazetteer prefers the reading Nudha, which removes the "Budha" that Mirchandani connects with a Buddhist country.

gaz_identification: Chach's assault on Kandabil c. 635-636; tribute
local_evidence: Chach prepared to storm Kandabil; the people took refuge in the fort, then agreed to pay 100,000 dirhams and 100 hill horses yearly; date c. 635-636, after his Kirman expedition.
quote: they agreed to pay him an annual tribute of 100,000 … The date of this … event may approximately be fixed at about 635-636
note: Kachhi pp. 24-25. Kachhi an independent fortified town forced into tribute only c. 635; Xuanzang (c. 641?) says nothing of 阿軬荼's subjection.

gaz_identification: Arab expeditions against Kandabil (684-841)
local_evidence: Kandabil was despoiled under Abdul Malik (684-705), fully conquered after Muhammad Qasim, refuge of the sons of Muhallab (720-24), taken by Imran (833-41) who moved its people to Khuzdar; one of the Arabs' principal cantonments.
quote: Several expeditions were m«ade against Kandabil during … the time of the Arab invasions
note: Kachhi p. 25.

gaz_identification: Ibn Haukal: Budha between Turan, Makran and Multan, capital Kandabel = Gandava
local_evidence: Ibn Haukal places Nudha/Budha between Turan, Makran and Multan with capital Kandabel, the modern Gandava; Hughes-Buller infers the kingdom included the Kachhi plain, some hills and part of Sind; inhabitants Nudha and Mand, i.e. Jats.
quote: capital was Randabcl or Kandail, the modem Gandiiva in … the Kachhi plain
note: Kachhi p. 27.

gaz_identification: Pre-Muhammadan settlement mounds near Bellpat
authority_cited: Stein, Report of Archaeological Survey Work NWFP and Baluchistan 1904-05
local_evidence: The mounds of Chhalgari, 8 miles SW of Bellpat station, visited by Stein in 1904, contain debris of a pre-Muhammadan settlement; main mound c. 175 yards long, pottery and small terracotta figurines.
quote: the mounds contain debris, accumulations of a pre -Muhammadan sctllemenL
note: Kachhi pp. 25-26. A pre-Islamic town in Kachhi (Mirchandani's 阿軬荼), undated; no Buddhist structure described.

gaz_identification: Two Buddhist clay seal impressions with five stūpas, 8th-9th c.
local_evidence: Two identical Buddhist seal impressions found at Tambu in Bhag in 1903 bear the ye dharmā formula in Brāhmī above five stūpas with umbrellas; Stein dates the script not older than the 8th nor much later than the 9th century.
quote: Buddhisf seal impressions were found a! the village … of Tambu in Bhag in 1903 … not older … than the eighth century A.D. nor much later than the ninth
note: Kachhi p. 26. The only dated Buddhist object in these volumes: votive sealings in Kachhi in the 8th-9th c., i.e. Buddhists in Kachhi after Xuanzang. Consistent with a Buddhist 阿軬荼 there (Mirchandani), but small portable objects; Middle Sindh also had Buddhists.

gaz_identification: Buddhist remains; Chachnāma: Buddhism dominant in 7th-c. Sind
local_evidence: Buddhist archaeological remains have been found in Kachhi, and according to the Chachnama Buddhism was the dominant religion in Sind in the 7th century.
quote: Buddhist archaeological remains have … also been found in the district and, according … Buddhism was the dominant religion in Sind in the sev
note: Kachhi p. 28.

gaz_identification: Khuzdar chief town of Arab Turan, with a small fortress
local_evidence: Khuzdar, at the junction of roads from Multan (Mula pass), Makran and Kandahar, was important to the Arabs; it was chief town of Turan, protected by a small fortress (probably Halwai peak); Biladuri quotes a poet praising Kusdar; spellings Kusdar, Kisdar, Kosdar.
quote: In the time of … the Arabs, it was the chief town of the small territory of Tdiun and … was protected by a small fortress
note: Jhalawan p. 34. Supports Khuzdar as the old centre of Turan (Mirchandani's capital of 臂多勢羅); the gazetteer gives no pre-Arab antiquity or Buddhist remains there. It also floats Krateros's Choarene = Khuzdar.

gaz_identification: Arab capture of Khuzdar while conquering Nukan and Kikan (c. 664)
local_evidence: c. 664 Al Manzar, appointed to the Indian frontier, while conquering Nukan and Kikan captured Khuzdar; c. 976 Ibn Haukal found Khuzdar governed by an Arab residing in Kaikanan; the Rai dynasty's territories reached the Kaikanan hills, near Kalat, suggested to be Nal.
quote: while conquering Nukan and Kikjln, captured Khnzdar … Kaikanan was soiiie\Yhere in the iicighbonrhood of Kalat and … it is suggested that it is identifiable with the modern Nil
note: Jhalawan pp. 34-35. Kikan/Kaikanan placed in Jhalawan (Nal), close to Khuzdar; neither Quetta-Pishin (Cunningham, Mirchandani) nor Waziristan (Stein).

gaz_identification: Nal identical with Kaikanan; many mounds
local_evidence: Historically Nal is identical with Kaikanan, and its many mounds (Sohr-damb and others) show its former importance.
quote: Ilistorically, Nal is identical with Kaikandn, and the numerous … mounds which exist indicate its importance in days gone by
note: Jhalawan p. 221. The firmest statement of the Nal equation; if 稽疆那 = Arab Kīkān, this puts it far south (Jhalawan), awkward for Xuanzang's 稽疆那 W of 伐剌拏 under either Bannu or Duki.

gaz_identification: Prehistoric (pre-Christian) pottery at Nal
local_evidence: Pottery dug from the Sohr damb near Nal in 1903 was judged by Marshall Indian or semi-Indian and probably pre-Christian, unlike anything from the Buddhist sites of Baluchistan or the Frontier.
quote: nothing at all like them is knovfu to have come from any of the … Buddhist sites in Baluchistan or the Frontier Province
note: Jhalawan pp. 60-61. Nal mounds prehistoric; no early-medieval or Buddhist finds at Kaikanan.

gaz_identification: Ancient kiln for glazed pottery at Khuzdar
local_evidence: A. Gupte found at Miri Butt in Khuzdar an ancient kiln for glazed pottery with pieces of potter's wheels; Kufic inscription at Khuzdar of the 4th-5th c. AH; Ghaznavid coins.
quote: found an anciout kiln for turning out … glazed pottery at Miri Butt in Khuzdar
note: Jhalawan pp. 59-60, 62. Same site as Hargreaves' Mini Butt (AR 1925-26); glazed ware and Kufic/Ghaznavid finds point to the Islamic period, not to a 7th-c. Buddhist capital.

gaz_identification: Lakorian as a tract of land in Jhalawan
local_evidence: Lakorian appears only as land held by the Gwahranjau section of the Sasolis (and in a list of the Sardar's grants); no ruined city is mentioned.
quote: The Gwahriinjau section own lauds in Lakorian
note: Jhalawan p. 80 (also pp. 79, Appendix grants). The gazetteer does not mention the "great ruined city" of Lākoriān on which Cunningham/Mizutani rest 窣菟黎濕伐羅; silence, not refutation.

gaz_identification: Rock-cut cave vault W of Pandran
local_evidence: A cave west of Pandran has an underground vault of a front chamber and two recesses hewn out of conglomerate rock; bones and a bed were found.
quote: The whole appears to have been hewn out … of the coaglohiorato rock
note: Jhalawan pp. 59-60. Rock-cut chamber, undated, no religious features; noted for the cave enquiry.

gaz_identification: Hindu temple of Kali below the Kalat citadel, probably pre-Muhammadan
local_evidence: Below the Kalat citadel lies a Hindu temple of Kali, probably pre-Muhammadan; the marble goddess holding the emblem of plenty stands before two perpetual lamps.
quote: Below i!ic citadel lies a Hindu temple of Kdli, probably … of pre-Muhammadan date
note: Sarawan p. 230 (also IGI p. 164). Śākta shrine in Kalat ("Kalat-i-Sewa"); date asserted, not shown.

gaz_identification: Chach's march via Armabel through Makran to the Kirman boundary (635-6)
local_evidence: Rai Chach marched in 635-6 to fix his boundary with Kirman: via Armabel, whose chief received him, through Makran; beyond Makran and the hills he rebuilt an old fort Kanarpur, then set the boundary between Makran and Kirman at a river, planting date trees.
quote: he' marched towards Annabel, § and when he … arrived there, the chief of the place came to receive him … Chach proceeded from thence to Makrdn
note: Makran p. 42. Makran (to the Kirman border) claimed by Sind c. 635. Mirchandani's Laṅgala in Persian Makran would then be Sindhi, while Xuanzang says 狼揭羅 obeyed Persia; the gazetteer itself notes Sasanian control just before (Khusrau Parviz).

gaz_identification: Makran in Sind's possession at the Arab invasions; Arab conquest 643-4
local_evidence: Makran was in Sind's possession when the Arabs came; in the last year of Umar's caliphate Abdulla bin Abdulla invaded and defeated the ruler of Makran, Malik Sad, who had reinforcements from Sind.
quote: Makrdn, therefore, must have been in possession of Sind … when the Arab invasions took place
note: Makran pp. 42-43.

gaz_identification: Kaikanan probably near Nal; Arab campaigns there
local_evidence: While Taghar bin Dair was reducing Kaikanan (probably near Nal) Ali was assassinated; the Arabs were later completely defeated near Kaikanan; Rashid made a successful inroad on it.
quote: the reduction of Kaikdndn (which is probably in the: … neighbourhood of the modern Ndl)
note: Makran p. 44. Same placement as Jhalawan volume.

gaz_identification: Ibn Haukal: ruler of Makran resided at Kiz, half the size of Multan
local_evidence: In the 10th century Ibn Haukal notes the ruler was an Arab residing in Kiz (Kech), half the size of Multan; Holdich identified the ruins near Kalatuk as Kiz; papers by Holdich and Haig identify Persian-Makran places of the Arabs incl. Kasrkand.
quote: established his residence in … the city of Kiz (K6ch), which was about half the size of … Multdn
note: Makran pp. 45, 57. The chief town of Arab Makran was Kech, in British (eastern) Makran; Kasrkand (Mirchandani's capital) only listed among Persian-Makran places.

gaz_identification: Old pilgrim route Las Bela → Kech valley → Persian Makran via Pishin, Goh and Kasarkand
local_evidence: The old pilgrim route from India via Las Bela to the west crosses the Jaulak and runs the length of the Kech valley into Persian Makran via Pishin, Goh and Kasarkand; still much frequented.
quote: The old pilgrim route from India via Las Bdla … to the west crosses the Jaulak and traverses the whole … length of the Kdch valley leading into Persian Makrdn via … Pishin, G6h and Kasarkand
note: Makran p. 298. Confirms the road Mirchandani has Xuanzang's hearsay follow from Bela to Kasarkand (along the Kech valley); does not show Kasarkand was a capital or had a Śiva temple.

gaz_identification: Island shrine of Kali Devi off the Makran coast, linked to Hinglaj
local_evidence: Haptalar island is to Hindus Satadip, abode of the goddess Kali Devi, who spends seven watches there and the eighth bathing at Hinglaj; the Arabs called it Astalo; pilgrims visit and sacrifice goats.
quote: the abode of … the goddess Kdli D&vi who remains there for seven out of … Only in the morning does she leave it to take her bath at … Hingldj
note: Makran pp. 278-279. A second Devī tīrtha on this coast tied to Hinglaj; Arab name attested, so pre-modern. Śākta, not a liṅga.

gaz_identification: Early history obscure; record begins with Timur (1383)
local_evidence: The earlier history of Loralai is obscure and can only be surmised from the provincial history; the narrative begins c. 1383 with Timur.
quote: earlier history of the portion of Baluchistan em … braced within the present Loralai District is involved in … obscurity
note: Loralai p. 32. No 7th-c. record for Mirchandani's 伐剌拏 (Bolan–Loralai, capital near Duki).

gaz_identification: Mounds and old forts near Chotiali, Tharu and Duki ascribed to Hindus
local_evidence: Duke (1883): lofty mounds in Thal are old castles like the Hindu forts at Kalat-i-Nasir Khan; the hill country from Kashmir to Makran was once ruled by a Hindu Raja (Sihar/Sihan); ancient ruins near Chotiali, Tharu and Duki; large old bricks.
quote: the whole hill country from Kashmir to Mekran … was ruled by a Hindu R<ija, whose title was bihar or Sihan
note: Loralai p. 44. Pre-Islamic settlement in Mirchandani's Duki area asserted from form of mounds; no Buddhist or datable remains.

gaz_identification: Ruined hill forts, no religious remains (Stein 1904)
local_evidence: Stein found the ruins called "Monastery Hill" near Loralai to be two refuge forts of coursed stone; no carved stonework or anything suggesting a religious purpose.
quote: Of carved stonework I could find no trace, nor any … remains which could possibly suggest a religious purpose
note: Loralai pp. 45-46. The one site in Loralai with a monastic name is not a monastery; Stein's Kushan stūpa (1926-27) came later.

gaz_identification: Largest ancient mound on the Frontier; prehistoric to Islamic
local_evidence: The Dabarkot mound, 10 miles SE of Duki, c. 80 ft high, is the largest ancient mound Stein knew on the Frontier; probably prehistoric at base, with glazed sherds on top and a hoard of c. 200 Muslim silver coins.
quote: it is certainly the largest ancient mound known to me on … the Frontier
note: Loralai p. 47. Long occupation near Duki; nothing specific to the 7th c.

gaz_identification: Little known before the 13th c.
local_evidence: Pishin is first mentioned in the Avesta; Krateros may have passed via Quetta; little is known of Quetta-Pishin up to the 13th century, when it formed part of the Ghaznavid kingdom.
quote: We know little of the history of Quetta-Pishin up to the … thirteenth century A.D.
note: Quetta-Pishin p. 31. No Kaikanan/Kikan in the history chapter; the gazetteer does not adopt Cunningham's Pishin = Kīkān (contrast the Jhalawan volume's Nal).

gaz_identification: Village Kikani in Quetta tahsil
local_evidence: Kikani (743 inhabitants) is among the most important villages of the Quetta tahsil.
quote: Kotwal (746), Kikani (743), Sra Ghurgi (730)
note: Quetta tahsil miniature gazetteer. A modern village name echoing Kīkān in Quetta itself; the gazetteer draws no connection. Name evidence only, could favour Cunningham/Mirchandani's Quetta–Pishin for 稽疆那.

gaz_identification: Largest ancient mound in Pishin; no structures or coins
local_evidence: Stein: Pishin is the oldest historically attested oasis of Baluchistan; Riasa Ghundi, c. 60 ft high, consists of culture strata with hard coarse pottery and painted sherds; no structural remains or coins.
quote: The plain of Pishin is the oldest historically attested oasis of … Baluchistan
note: Quetta-Pishin pp. 47-48. No early-medieval or Buddhist remains in Pishin.

gaz_identification: Shrine of a Nath yogi; Shivratri fair since 1892
local_evidence: Shrine of Pani Nath, a disciple of Gorakhnath, within Quetta fort; Hindus worship there on Mondays and an annual Shivratri fair has been held since 1892.
quote: The shrines of Pani Natli, a Hindu Yogi, lies within the … walls of the fort
note: Quetta-Pishin p. 345. Modern Śaiva/Nāth cult; no bearing on dating.

gaz_identification: Bibi Nani = Hinglaj goddess = Nanaia (Masson); spring called Mahadev
local_evidence: Bibi Nani, guardian of the Bolan water supply, is also the Muslim name of the Hinglaj goddess; Masson links it with Nanaia of the Persians and Bactrians; a related spring is Ghaib Pir to Muslims and Mahadev to the Hindus of Kachhi.
quote: goddess of the shrine at Hinglaj, who is also known to … Muhammadans as Bibi Nani … known as Ghaib Pir by the Muhammadans … and as Mahadev by the Hindus of Eachhi
note: Bolan pp. 37-38. Nani/Hinglaj cult extends to the Bolan; Mahadev name for a spring; no early date. The Bolan history knows nothing before the Arghuns (1486).
